# Methodology

## Data Dictionary 

## Raw Data to Clean Data

The first step of cleaning the raw data was to combine every individual data file together. We then made use of tidyverse methods, such as mutate() to separate columns which had multiple variables in the same column, such as Age Group and Age Grade. The Parkrun variable was obtained using the file name from each dataset, and similarly, the Week variable was calculated using iteration, resetting to 1 after the location a Parkrun took place changes.

The next was cleaning the Parkrunner column, and anonymising the data. The parkrunner column was very untidy, being incredibly verbose and hard to read, while still containing useful data, such as milestone data. It also contained the names of each runner, which is a massive privacy risk. By separating the variables into different columns, anonymising the data using a Caesar Cipher, we could ensure that the all the relevant data remained, and the name's of each runner remained obscured.

The final step was to clean for the time variables. There are three variables that were stored in Time, that being the time to complete a race, the personal best time set by a runner for that location, and whether or not that was their first time running that parkrun. By separating the columns, we could obtain information regarding repeat runners, how many runners were first timers, etc. 

By taking these steps, we were able to produce a tidy dataset which contained all of the relevant data for answering the key questions set by Puma.

## Key Questions

### Question one 

Question: Which Parkrun provides the best marketing opportunity with the largest number of people ?

To find out which Parkrun is best for Puma’s marketing, I compared how many people take part in each location.  
I used the cleaned data to count total number of runs (including repeats), and number of unique runners, each person only counted once, excluding unknown IDs.  

I then created two bar charts to show these results — one for **unique runners** and another for **total finishes**.  
The first chart helps show which Parkrun has the biggest overall audience, while the second shows which Parkrun is the most active.  
This comparison helps find the place where advertising would reach the most people.

### Question 2  
Question: Do new people come each week or is it always the same people?

I wanted to see if Parkrun keeps getting new runners each week or if it’s mostly the same people coming back.  
I looked at each runner’s `name_id` and marked them as **new** the first time they appeared, and as **returning** if they had joined before.  

Then I calculated the total number of runners and how many were new in each week, and worked out the percentage of new runners.  
I made two plots — one showing how many new runners joined each week and another showing the percentage of new participants.  
This helped me understand if Parkrun keeps attracting new people or mainly has a stable, repeating group.

### Question Three (Daniel)

Question: Do people move between Parkruns? Does this mean if you advertise at fewer places you eventually
see people from other locations?

In order to answer this question, I went about determining how many locations different runners have been to. Results showed that 26.6% of runners have gone to another location. I then used a bar chart to determine how many people have been to different numbers of Parkruns. 

My interpretation of the second half of the question, is that it has to do with audience overlap. Essentially, if runners had bought Puma products due to advertising at one location, would those customers appear in other locations, where the advertisements would have little to no effect? I came to the conclusion that more audience overlap means that advertising at more locations would have diminishing returns on the financial investment, and recommended advertising at more popular locations.

### Question Six (Daniel)

Question: Does the distance between Parkrun locations predict the amount of mixing of people between those
locations?

In order to answer this question, I first obtained the geographical coordinates for each Parkrun. Using the sf and leaflet libraries, I could then obtain the distances between each location (straight line, point-to-point), as a matrix, which I converted to a data frame.

I then created a new df mixing_pairs, which connected every Parkrun to every other Parkrun in pairwise relationships. Using this, and a runner_locations summary to determine the locations each runner has been to, I obtained a sort of mixing score; the number of runners that have been to both locations in a pair. Using the mixing score, and joining it with the distance data frame to obtain a data frame with a distance and a score for each pair of Parkruns (distance_mixing). I could then create a predictive model, using glm() with family = Gamma.



## Limitations of the Dataset

Audience Identification (Q1):Some runners were listed as “UNK” or had no name ID, so I couldn’t tell if they were new or repeat participants.That means the number of unique runners might be a bit lower than the real value.Also, if a person’s name ID was entered differently across weeks, they could have been counted twice by mistake.

New and Returning Runners (Q2):This question depends a lot on having the same name ID every week.If someone’s ID was missing or typed differently, the code would treat them as a new runner even if they’d come before.The data also only covers a short period of 11 weeks, so it might not show the long-term pattern of new people joining or old runners returning.

Marketing Knowledge (Q3): My knowledge of marketing is very limited, and the research I did, while very informative, does not give me full confidence in a correct conclusion.

Distances (Q6): The issue with calculating if distance predicts mixing between two Parkruns, is an issue of realism. The distances I measured were just straight lines from Parkrun to Parkrun. As such, the possible mixing scores are not reflective of real world travel distances, such as road layouts, traffic, etc. As such, two Parkruns may be very far from each other, but if it takes very little time to get between them, there may be more mixing present. 

Non-Normal Data (Q6): The distance_mixing data frame was not Normal data, and was heaviliy right-skewed. As such, I could not fit a typical linear model, and had to use a Gamma distribution, which produced the best results in terms of residuals and QQ-plot.

## Future Improvements and Development

**Question 1:**  
If I had more data, I’d look at extra factors like location size, weather, and population to see what makes some Parkruns attract more people than others.  
It would also help to include demographic data so Puma could target the right type of customers.  
Creating an interactive dashboard would make it easier to compare locations visually.

**Question 2:**  
To understand participation better, a longer time period would be useful to see long-term trends instead of just 11 weeks.  
Making sure every runner has a consistent ID would also make the results more reliable.  
With more data, I could even build a simple model to predict when new runners are most likely to appear.
